claim: More than 90% of breast cancer-related deaths are due to metastasis.
source: More than 90% of breast cancer-related deaths are due to metastasis (Fahad Ullah, 2019; Park et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Fahad Ullah, 2019; Park et al., 2022).

claim: Current treatments including endocrine therapy, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy are ineffective in preventing breast cancer metastasis.
source: Current treatments, including endocrine therapy, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy, are ineffective in preventing breast cancer metastasis and remain the greatest clinical challenge for breast cancer treatment (Barzaman et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barzaman et al., 2020.

claim: Cancer metastasis is associated with epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT).
source: Cancer metastasis is associated with a process called epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) (Mittal, 2018; Lüönd et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mittal, 2018; Lüönd et al., 2021).

claim: EMT is a pre-metastatic state in which epithelial cells lose their tight junctions and convert to migratory mesenchymal cells.
source: EMT is a pre-metastatic state in which epithelial cells lose their tight junctions and convert to migratory mesenchymal cells (Dongre and Weinberg, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dongre and Weinberg, 2019.

claim: Metastatic invasion is a highly energy-intensive process.
source: Metastatic invasion is a highly energy-intensive process (Mosier et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mosier et al., 2021.

claim: Metabolic reprogramming during the EMT process contributes to metastasis and tumorigenesis.
source: It has become increasingly recognized that metabolic reprogramming during the EMT process contributes to metastasis and tumorigenesis (Kang et al., 2019; Sciacovelli and Frezza, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kang et al., 2019; Sciacovelli and Frezza, 2017).

claim: Lipid metabolic reprogramming plays a critical role in meeting the energy requirements of metastatic invasion.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that lipid metabolic reprogramming plays a critical role in meeting the energy requirements of metastatic invasion (Bian et al., 2021; Li et al., 2020; Snaebjornsson et al., 2020; Cheng et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Bian et al., 2021; Li et al., 2020; Snaebjornsson et al., 2020; Cheng et al., 2018).

claim: Lipid droplets (LDs) accumulation is associated with aggressiveness in many cancer types.
source: lipid droplets (LDs) accumulation is associated with aggressiveness in many cancer types (Antunes et al., 2022), including breast (Zembroski et al., 2021), brain (Taïb et al., 2019), liver (Niu et al., 2021), lung (Jin and Yuan, 2020), and prostate (Roman et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies across different cancer types.

claim: The aggregation of FAs in LDs is considered a priming state to prepare for metastasis.
source: Indeed, the aggregation of FAs in LDs is considered a priming state to prepare for metastasis (Petan, 2020; Rozeveld et al., 2020; Senga et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Petan, 2020; Rozeveld et al., 2020; Senga et al., 2018).

claim: FAs stored in LDs were a crucial resource in fueling the metastatic process in pancreatic cancer.
source: For example, it has been reported that FAs stored in LDs were a crucial resource in fueling the metastatic process in pancreatic cancer (Rozeveld et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rozeveld et al., 2020.

claim: Metastatic triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) depends on FAO to produce high adenosine triphosphate (ATP) levels.
source: Additionally, previous studies have suggested that metastatic triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) depends on FAO to produce high adenosine triphosphate (ATP) levels (Camarda et al., 2016; Wright et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Camarda et al., 2016; Wright et al., 2017).

claim: ACSL4 catalyzes the conversion of long-chain FAs to acyl-CoAs.
source: ACSL4 catalyzes the conversion of long-chain FAs to acyl-CoAs, a necessary step for free long-chain FAs to enter the next metabolic pathway (Kuwata and Hara, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kuwata and Hara, 2019, and represents established knowledge about ACSL4 function.

claim: ACSL4 is a well-known biomarker of ferroptosis.
source: The increased expression and activity of ACSL4 have been observed in many cancer types and it is well-known biomarkers of ferroptosis (Doll et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Doll et al., 2017.

claim: ACSL4 promotes hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cell proliferation and metastasis via lipogenesis and LDs accumulation.
source: For example, ACSL4 promotes hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cell proliferation and metastasis via lipogenesis and LDs accumulation (Niu et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Niu et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2020).

claim: In prostate cancer, ACSL4 promotes cell growth, invasion, and hormonal resistance.
source: In prostate cancer, ACSL4 promotes cell growth, invasion, and hormonal resistance (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2015.

claim: The function of ACSL4 in breast cancer has been implicated in hormone therapy resistance involving the regulation of energy-dependent transporter expression.
source: The function of ACSL4 in breast cancer has been implicated in hormone therapy resistance involving the regulation of energy-dependent transporter expression (Orlando et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Orlando et al., 2019.

claim: ZEB2 and ACSL4 were among the top 200 upregulated genes (>twofold) in drug-resistant breast cancer cells.
source: We noticed that the rate-limiting enzymes of FA metabolism, long-chain fatty acyl synthetase 4 (ACSL4), and EMT transcription factor ZEB2 were among the top 200 upregulated (>twofold) genes (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data presented in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: ACSL4 expression was positively correlated with ZEB2 expression in TCGA database (r = 0.7657, p < 0.001).
source: To verify these findings in the clinical sample, we analyzed ZEB2 and ACSL4 expression in TCGA database and found that ACSL4 expression was positively correlated with ZEB2 expression (Figure 1B, r = 0.7657, p < 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA database data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ACSL4 expression was inversely correlated with ERα expression in TCGA database (r = −0.3312, p < 0.001).
source: and inversely correlated with ERα expression (Figure 1C, r = −0.3312, p < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA database data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Patients with higher ACSL4 or ZEB2 expression had worse prognosis than those with lower expression.
source: We found that patients with higher ACSL4 or ZEB2 expression, especially those with simultaneous high expression had worse prognosis than those with lower expression (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: Basal-like and taxol-resistant cell lines showed high expression of ZEB2 and ACSL4.
source: To confirm this correlation, we performed western blot analysis and found that basal-like and taxol-resistant cell lines, which lack ERα expression, showed high expression of ZEB2 and ACSL4, whereas low or no ZEB2 and ACSL4 expression was detected in luminal subtype cell lines (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The expression of ACSL4 was positively correlated with ZEB2 expression in immunohistochemistry analysis (p < 0.001).
source: The immunohistochemistry staining assay, as shown in Figure 1H–J, also confirmed that the expression of ACSL4 was positively correlated with ZEB2 expression (Figure 1H, p < 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The expression of ACSL4 was inversely correlated with ERα expression in immunohistochemistry analysis (p < 0.001).
source: and inversely correlated with ERα expression (Figure 1I, p < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Overexpression of ACSL4 significantly enhanced the metastatic and invasive capacities of MCF-7 cells.
source: The overexpression of ACSL4 significantly enhanced the metastatic and invasive capacities of MCF-7 cells (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by wound healing and transwell invasion assay data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: ACSL4 knockdown by shRNA significantly reduced the metastatic and invasive capacities of MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Conversely, ACSL4 knockdown by shRNA significantly reduced the metastatic and invasive capacities of MDA-MB-231 cells compared to that of the control cells (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by wound healing and transwell invasion assay data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: ACSL4 knockdown cells had a significantly smaller length to width ratio than control cells (p < 0.05).
source: Interestingly, the Phalloidin staining showed that the ACSL4 knockdown cells had a significantly smaller length to width ratio, which indicates the reversion of EMT process, than those of the control group (p < 0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of ZEB2 significantly enhanced the metastatic and invasive capacities of MCF-7 cells.
source: We also observed that overexpression of ZEB2 significantly enhanced the metastatic and invasive capacities of MCF-7 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by wound healing and transwell invasion assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: The metastatic and invasive abilities of MDA-MB-231 cells were significantly reduced in ZEB2 knockdown cells.
source: Conversely, the metastatic and invasive abilities of MDA-MB-231 cells were significantly reduced in ZEB2 knockdown cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by wound healing and transwell invasion assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and 2D.

claim: The tight junction and focal adhesion pathways were among the most upregulated pathways in ACSL4 knockdown cells.
source: To investigate the downstream genes regulated by ACSL4, we performed RNA-sequencing analysis and identified that the tight junction and focal adhesion pathways were among the most upregulated pathways in ACSL4 knockdown cells compared to control cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data and KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: After silencing of ACSL4 and ZEB2, the luminal epithelial marker E-cadherin was increased, whereas the mesenchymal markers vimentin and N-cadherin were decreased.
source: To verify the RNA-seq results, we examined the expression of adhesion-related genes by immunoblotting and found that after silencing of ACSL4 and ZEB2, the luminal epithelial marker E-cadherin was increased, whereas the mesenchymal markers, such as vimentin and N-cadherin were decreased (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Overexpression of ACSL4 significantly restored the invasive and metastatic capacities of ZEB2 knockdown cells by 35.1% and 32.4%, respectively.
source: As expected, overexpression of ACSL4 significantly restored the invasive and metastatic capacities of ZEB2 knockdown cells by 35.1% and 32.4%, respectively (Figure 2I, J), indicating that ACSL4 is essential for ZEB2-mediated breast cancer invasion and migration.
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell invasion and wound healing assay data shown in Figure 2I and 2J.

claim: The basal number and size of LDs were significantly larger in MDA-MB-231 and Taxol-resistant MCF-7 cells.
source: Thus, we measured the basal LDs content of breast cancer cells, including MCF-7, MDA-MB-231, and Taxol-resistant MCF-7 cells. The basal number and size of LDs were significantly larger in MDA-MB-231 and Taxol-resistant MCF-7 cells, both of which are highly invasive breast cancer cell lines (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by BODIPY 493/503 staining data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ACSL4 co-localized with LDs in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Fluorescence microscopy revealed that ACSL4 co-localized with LDs in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ACSL4 knockdown reduced cytoplasmic LDs abundance and LDs-containing cells in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Notably, ACSL4 knockdown reduced cytoplasmic LDs abundance and LDs-containing cells in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by BODIPY 493/503 staining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cytoplasmic LDs abundance and LDs-containing cells were significantly reduced in ZEB2-depleted cells.
source: Consistently, cytoplasmic LDs abundance and LDs-containing cells were significantly reduced in ZEB2-depleted cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by BODIPY 493/503 staining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ACSL4 knockdown breast cancer cells had a reduced ability to incorporate long-strain monounsaturated and saturated FAs into TG and phospholipids.
source: Untargeted lipidomic analyses revealed that ACSL4 knockdown breast cancer cells had a reduced ability to incorporate long-strain monounsaturated (18:1, 17:1, 22:1, 24:1, and 26:1) and saturated FAs (16:0, 18:0, 24:0, and 26:0) into TG and phospholipids, indicating that ACSL4 promotes the incorporation of long-chain monounsaturated and saturated FAs into TG and phospholipids in these cells (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by untargeted lipidomic analysis data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: All lipids including TG, phospholipids, and cholesterol esters had decreased incorporation of several polyunsaturated FAs in ACSL4-depleted cells.
source: Moreover, all these lipids, including TG, phospholipids, and cholesterol esters, had decreased incorporation of several polyunsaturated FAs, such as 22:6, 20:4, 22:4, and 22:5, in ACSL4-depleted cells as reported previously (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A; Doll et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, and is consistent with previous reports (Doll et al., 2017).

claim: Treatment with oleic acid (OA) dramatically enhanced LDs abundance in breast cancer cells.
source: Exogenous oleic acid (OA) was added to the cell culture medium. Treatment with OA dramatically enhanced LDs abundance in the cells (Figure 4A), indicating that breast cancer cells tend to store lipids in LDs for energy reserves.
evidence: The claim is supported by BODIPY 493/503 staining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: OA-treated cells exhibited significantly enhanced invasive and metastatic capacities compared with control cells.
source: Next, we assessed the effects of exogenous OA treatment on cell migration. Transwell and wound healing assays revealed that OA-treated cells exhibited significantly enhanced invasive and metastatic capacities compared with control cells (Figure 4B, C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell invasion and wound healing assay data shown in Figure 4B, 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The addition of oleic acid (OA) restores the invasive and metastatic capacities of ACSL4 knockdown cells by 33.12% and 18.61%, respectively.
source: As expected, the addition of oleic acid (OA) obviously restores the invasive and metastatic capacities of ACSL4 knockdown cells by 33.12% and 18.61%, respectively (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell invasion and wound healing assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The lipid signal was significantly decreasing in the leading edge of the scratch of the wound healing migration.
source: We observed that the lipid signal was significantly decreasing in the leading edge of the scratch of the wound healing migration (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by BODIPY 493/503 staining data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Significantly reduced LDs were observed in cells on the lower side of the transwell chamber.
source: In addition, we observed significantly reduced LDs in cells on the lower side of the transwell chamber, suggesting that lipids stored in LDs were utilized and degraded during cell migration and invasion (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by BODIPY 493/503 staining data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The FAO pathway was among the top 20 regulated pathways in ACSL4 knockdown cells.
source: To explore the mechanisms by which ACSL4 regulates lipid metabolism, we performed RNA-sequencing to investigate downstream pathways and genes regulated by ACSL4. KEGG enrichment analysis revealed that the FAO pathway was among the top 20 regulated pathways (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data and KEGG enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ACSL4 knockdown reduced the expression of genes involved in the FAO pathways.
source: ACSL4 knockdown reduced the expression of genes involved in the FAO pathways (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The FAO rate-limiting enzyme CPT1A was significantly reduced in ACSL4 knockdown cells.
source: Importantly, we observed that the FAO rate-limiting enzyme CPT1A was significantly reduced in ACSL4 knockdown cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Deletion of ACSL4 significantly reduced the expression of CPT1A, but did not affect the expression of CPT1B and CPT1C.
source: Reverse transcription PCR (The polymerase chain reaction) confirmed that deletion of ACSL4 significantly reduced the expression of CPT1A, but did not affect the expression of CPT1B and CPT1C (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ACSL4 silencing reduced CPT1A protein expression.
source: Consistently, ACSL4 silencing reduced CPT1A protein expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The levels of ATGL, FASN, and SREBP2 were significantly decreased after ACSL4 knockdown.
source: In addition, the levels of other lipid metabolic enzymes, such as ATGL, FASN, and SREBP2, were significantly decreased after ACSL4 knockdown (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The OCR derived from long-chain FAs was significantly reduced in ACSL4 or ZEB2-silencing cells.
source: Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) was calculated in ACSL4 or ZEB2-silencing and control cells. We observed that the OCR derived from long-chain FAs was significantly reduced in ACSL4 or ZEB2-silencing cells (Figure 5D, E), suggesting the metabolic advantage of increased long-chain FAO and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS).
evidence: The claim is supported by OCR measurement data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: ACSL4 or ZEB2 knockout cells had significantly reduced ATP generation compared to control cells.
source: Since OXPHOS is accompanied by increased ATP generation, we measured ATP levels and found that ACSL4 or ZEB2 knockout cells had significantly reduced ATP generation compared to control cells (Figure 5F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5F and 5G.

claim: There was no significant difference in lactate production between ACSL4 or ZEB2 knockdown and control cells.
source: To exclude OXPHOS derived from the aerobic glycolysis pathway, we measured lactate production and found no significant difference in lactate production between ACSL4 or ZEB2 knockdown and control cells, suggesting that glucose metabolism is not involved in ACSL4- or ZEB2-mediated metabolic process (Figure 5H, I).
evidence: The claim is supported by lactate measurement data shown in Figure 5H and 5I.

claim: Silencing of ZEB2 by siRNA in MDA-MB-231 cells significantly reduced ACSL4 mRNA levels and protein expression.
source: Silencing of ZEB2 by siRNA (Small interfering RNA) in MDA-MB-231 cells significantly reduced ACSL4 mRNA levels and protein expression in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and western blot data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The ACSL4 promoter contained four canonical ZEB2-binding E-boxes (CAGGT/CACCT) located at −287, −965, −1038, and −1116.
source: We found that the ACSL4 promoter contained four canonical ZEB2-binding E-boxes (CAGGT/CACCT) located at −287, −965, −1038, and −1116 of the ACSL4 promoter, respectively (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis of the ACSL4 promoter shown in Figure 6C.

claim: ZEB2 overexpression significantly enhanced the luciferase activity of all five E-box-containing segments of the ACSL4 promoter.
source: ZEB2 overexpression significantly enhanced the luciferase activity of all five E-box-containing segments of the ACSL4 promoter, whereas no significant change was observed in the control segment (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: ZEB2 binds to the E-box located at nucleotides −184 to −295 of the ACSL4 promoter.
source: Primer set 1, which covered segment 1, consistently exhibited apparent ZEB2 binding (Figure 6F, G). However, no binding was detectable using the other three sets of primers (Figure 6F), indicating that ZEB2 binds to the E-box located at nucleotides −184 to −295 of the ACSL4 promoter.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 6F and 6G.

claim: ACSL4 promoter activity was almost entirely abolished by mutations in the −287 E-box.
source: Since the −287 E-box exhibited apparent ZEB2 binding, we generated mutants of the −287 E-box promoter–luciferase construct. The luciferase reporter assay revealed that ACSL4 promoter activity was almost entirely abolished by the mutations (Figure 6H), suggesting that this promoter region is essential for ZEB2-mediated ACSL4 promoter activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Both ZEB2 mRNA and protein levels were reduced after the depletion of ACSL4 in two BCSC cell lines.
source: We then performed quantitative PCR and immunoblotting and observed that both ZEB2 mRNA and protein levels were reduced after the depletion of ACSL4 in the two BCSC cell lines (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and western blot data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: The expression of ACSL4 caused a significant decrease in the ubiquitination of ZEB2.
source: HEK293T cells were co-transfected with HA-ubiquitin and myc-ZEB2 expression vectors along with either an empty vector or an ACSL4 overexpression vector. As shown in Figure 7C, the expression of ACSL4 caused a significant decrease in the ubiquitination of ZEB2.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: An increasing ubiquitination of ZEB2 was observed in ACSL4 silencing cells.
source: Conversely, we observed a increasing ubiquitination of ZEB2 in ACSL4 silencing cells (Figure 7D), suggesting that ACSL4 attenuated the ubiquitin proteolysis of ZEB2.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assays and GST pull down assays revealed a specific interaction between ACSL4 and ZEB2 proteins.
source: Notably, co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assays and GST pull down assays revealed a specific interaction between ACSL4 and ZEB2 proteins, supporting the notion that ZEB2 and ACSL4 are present in a protein complex (Figure 7E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Co-IP and GST pull down assay data shown in Figure 7E, 7F, and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: ACSL4 and ZEB2 were co-localized in some certain regions of the cytoplasm.
source: Immunofluorescence assay revealed that ACSL4 and ZEB2 were co-localized in some certain regions of the cytoplasm (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Endogenous ZEB2 protein levels were almost completely suppressed in ACSL4 knockdown cells from 0 to 8 hr time points after cycloheximide treatment.
source: To further confirm the role of ACSL4 in the regulation of ZEB2 proteolysis, cycloheximide was added to the cell medium to block the synthesis of new proteins. Interestingly, endogenous ZEB2 protein levels were almost completely suppressed in ACSL4 knockdown cells from 0 to 8 hr time points (Figure 7G, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 7G and 7H.

claim: ZEB2 protein maintained a relatively steady level at 6 hr in ACSL4 overexpressing cells compared with control cells.
source: Conversely, ZEB2 protein maintained a relatively steady level at 6 hr in ACSL4 overexpressing cells compared with control cells that undergone obvious ZEB2 proteolysis at 4 hr after adding CHX, indicating an increased ZEB2 protein stability in ACSL4 overexpressing cells (Figure 7I, J).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 7I and 7J.

claim: Depletion of ACSL4 resulted in a significant reduction in tumor growth and lung colonization of highly metastatic MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: To further validate our in vitro findings, we examined the effect of ACSL4 on lung metastasis of breast cancer cells in an animal model. Depletion of ACSL4 resulted in a significant reduction in tumor growth and lung colonization of highly metastatic MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo xenograft experiment data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The control group showed significantly more lung metastatic nodules and rapid tumor growth.
source: In contrast, the control group showed significantly more lung metastatic nodules (Figure 8B) and rapid tumor growth (Figure 8C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo xenograft experiment data shown in Figure 8B, 8C, and 8D.

claim: Immunohistochemistry confirmed a striking downregulation of ACSL4, accompanied by ZEB2 and vimentin, in ACSL4 knockdown tumors.
source: Immunohistochemistry confirmed a striking downregulation of ACSL4, accompanied by ZEB2 and vimentin, compared to those in the control group (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: There was an obvious reduction in LDs accumulation in the ACSL4 depletion tissue compared to control tissue.
source: To further validate the role of LDs in ACSL4 high-expression cells, we examined LDs content in frozen sections of the two groups. Consistent with the in vitro results, there was an obvious reduction in LDs accumulation in the ACSL4 depletion tissue compared to that in control tissue (Figure 8F).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence assay data on frozen tissue sections shown in Figure 8F.

claim: ZEB2 activates ACSL4 expression by directly binding to the ACSL4 promoter.
source: Mechanistically, ZEB2 activates ACSL4 expression by directly binding to the ACSL4 promoter.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP assay and luciferase reporter assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ACSL4 stabilizes and upregulates ZEB2 via transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms.
source: ACSL4 stabilizes and upregulates ZEB2 via transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR, western blot, ubiquitination assay, and protein stability assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Overexpression of ZEB2 or ACSL4 is associated with worse prognosis in advanced breast cancer.
source: In addition, we also provide evidence that overexpression of ZEB2 or ACSL4 is associated with worse prognosis in advanced breast cancer.
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis of TCGA database data.

claim: ACSL4 not only promotes the intracellular lipogenesis and LDs accumulation but also enhances FAO and ATP production by upregulating CPT1A.
source: Notably, ACSL4 not only promotes the intracellular lipogenesis and LDs accumulation but also enhances FAO and adenosine triphosphate production by upregulating the FAO rate-limiting enzyme CPT1A (carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 isoform A).
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomic analysis, BODIPY staining, OCR measurements, ATP measurements, and gene expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ACSL4 knockdown significantly reduced metastatic lung nodes in vivo.
source: Finally, we demonstrated that ACSL4 knockdown significantly reduced metastatic lung nodes in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo xenograft experiment data showing reduced lung metastatic nodules.

claim: TGF-β activates fatty acid synthase (FASN) and forms a FASN–TGFβ1–FASN-positive loop in cisplatin-resistant cells.
source: For example, Transforming growth factor (TGF)-beta (TGF-β), a major driver of EMT, activates fatty acid synthase (FASN) and forms a FASN–TGFβ1–FASN-positive loop in cisplatin-resistant cells, resulting in EMT induction (Jiang et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2016; Hua et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Jiang et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2016; Hua et al., 2020).

claim: ACSL4 stabilizes the oncoprotein c-Myc via the ubiquitin–proteasome system.
source: Our results are consistent with a recent report that ACSL4 stabilizes the oncoprotein c-Myc via the ubiquitin–proteasome system (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2020.

claim: LDs recruit Numb through the AP2A/ACSL3 complex to promote Numb degradation.
source: Interestingly, a recent study reported that LDs recruit Numb through the AP2A/ACSL3 complex to promote Numb degradation (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2022.

claim: LDs-derived lipolysis provide acetyl-CoA for the epigenetic regulation of gene transcription.
source: A recent study reported that LDs-derived lipolysis provide acetyl-CoA for the epigenetic regulation of gene transcription (Ippolito et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ippolito et al., 2022.

claim: ACSL4 could act as a tumor suppressor or oncogene, depending on the specific cancer type and tissue environment.
source: Previous studies have reported that ACSL4 could act as a tumor suppressor or oncogene, depending on the specific cancer type and tissue environment (Cheng et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2021; Lei et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Grube et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Cheng et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2021; Lei et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Grube et al., 2022).

claim: ACSL4 has been shown to play an essential role in metastasis in many types of cancer.
source: Although ACSL4 has been shown to play an essential role in metastasis in many types of cancer (Wu et al., 2015; Maloberti et al., 2010; Sánchez-Martínez et al., 2017), its mechanism of ACSL4-mediated metastasis is not fully understood.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Wu et al., 2015; Maloberti et al., 2010; Sánchez-Martínez et al., 2017).

claim: The formation of LDs is required for FAO.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that fatty acids are stored in LDs before entering FAO, and the formation of LDs is required for FAO (Li et al., 2020; Petan, 2020; Welte and Gould, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Li et al., 2020; Petan, 2020; Welte and Gould, 2017).

claim: LDs undergo lipolysis during the process of migration in pancreatic cancer.
source: Our findings are in line with a recent study showing that LDs undergo lipolysis during the process of migration in pancreatic cancer (Rozeveld et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rozeveld et al., 2020.

claim: Hexokinase 2 enhances tumorigenicity by activating the ACSL4-mediated FA β-oxidation pathway.
source: Our results are in line with a recent study that reported that hexokinase 2 enhances tumorigenicity by activating the ACSL4-mediated FA β-oxidation pathway (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2022.

claim: FAO is a critical energy pathway in TNBC.
source: Our results reveal the mechanism of previous findings that FAO is a critical energy pathway in TNBC (Camarda et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Camarda et al., 2016.

claim: ACSL4 is a direct downstream target of ZEB2 in controlling lipid storage and LDs accumulation.
source: Importantly, our results demonstrate that ACSL4 is a direct downstream target of ZEB2 in controlling lipid storage and LDs accumulation, which are important steps and energy pools for metastasis.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP assay, luciferase reporter assay, and functional assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Elevated ACSL4 levels can be used as an effective marker for predicting cancer progression in patients with advanced breast cancer.
source: Elevated ACSL4 levels can be used as an effective marker for predicting cancer progression in patients with advanced breast cancer.
evidence: The claim is based on survival analysis data showing that high ACSL4 expression is associated with worse prognosis.

claim: ZEB2–ACSL4 signaling is an attractive therapeutic target for overcoming breast cancer metastasis.
source: Clinically, our findings identified ZEB2–ACSL4 signaling as an attractive therapeutic target for overcoming breast cancer metastasis.
evidence: The claim is based on the functional importance of the ZEB2-ACSL4 axis in breast cancer metastasis demonstrated in the study.

claim: ACSL4 is essential for ZEB2-mediated breast cancer invasion and migration.
source: As expected, overexpression of ACSL4 significantly restored the invasive and metastatic capacities of ZEB2 knockdown cells by 35.1% and 32.4%, respectively (Figure 2I, J), indicating that ACSL4 is essential for ZEB2-mediated breast cancer invasion and migration.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data showing that ACSL4 overexpression restores the invasive and metastatic capacities of ZEB2 knockdown cells.

claim: ACSL4 directs the long train of free FAs into lipid anabolism to form different lipid species in the LDs or other cellular membranes.
source: All together, these results suggest that ACSL4 directs the long train of free FAs into lipid anabolism to form different lipid species in the LDs or other cellular membranes.
evidence: The claim is based on lipidomic analysis data showing that ACSL4 promotes the incorporation of long-chain FAs into various lipid species.

claim: Lipids stored in LDs are a crucial resource to fuel the process of breast cancer invasion and migration.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that lipids stored in LDs are a crucial resource to fuel the process of breast cancer invasion and migration.
evidence: The claim is based on data showing that LDs decrease during migration and that exogenous FAs enhance migration.

claim: ACSL4 promotes FAO and ATP production by upregulating CPT1A.
source: We proposed that ACSL4 promotes FAO and ATP production by upregulating CPT1A, thereby providing energy support for breast cancer metastasis.
evidence: The claim is based on data showing that ACSL4 knockdown reduces CPT1A expression, FAO, and ATP production.

claim: At the pre-metastatic stage, ACSL4 enhances LDs accumulation by promoting lipogenesis.
source: Therefore, we propose a model in which cell migration is a multistep process accompanied by dynamic cellular lipid metabolic changes. At the pre-metastatic stage, ACSL4 enhances LDs accumulation by promoting lipogenesis.
evidence: The claim is based on data showing that ACSL4 promotes LDs accumulation and lipid synthesis.

claim: During metastasis, ACSL4 stimulates FAO to generate ATP.
source: During metastasis, ACSL4 stimulates FAO to generate ATP.
evidence: The claim is based on data showing that ACSL4 promotes FAO and ATP production, and that LDs decrease during migration.

claim: ZEB2 directly binds to the ACSL4 promoter to activate its mRNA expression.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that ZEB2 directly binds to the ACSL4 promoter to activate its mRNA expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP assay and luciferase reporter assay data.

claim: ACSL4 not only stabilizes the ZEB2 protein by attenuating its ubiquitination but also upregulates ZEB2 mRNA expression.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that ACSL4 not only stabilizes the ZEB2 protein by attenuating its ubiquitination but also upregulates ZEB2 mRNA expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay, protein stability assay, and qPCR data.

claim: ACSL4 regulates ZEB2 through both transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms.
source: Therefore, ACSL4 regulates ZEB2 through both transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that ACSL4 affects both ZEB2 mRNA levels and protein stability.

claim: The relationship between ZEB2 and ACSL4 forms a positive feedback loop.
source: Notably, the relationship between ZEB2 and ACSL4 could form a positive feedback loop: ZEB2 transcriptionally activates ACSL4, and conversely, ACSL4 stabilizes the ZEB2 protein by reducing its ubiquitination.
evidence: The claim is based on data showing that ZEB2 activates ACSL4 transcription and ACSL4 stabilizes ZEB2 protein.

claim: Amplification of either ZEB2 or ACSL4 might lock the positive feedback loop in an active state, resulting in enhanced invasive and metastatic capabilities of breast cancer cells.
source: Amplification of either gene might therefore lock this loop in an active state, resulting in the enhanced invasive and metastatic capabilities of breast cancer cells (Figure 8G).
evidence: The claim is based on the positive feedback loop mechanism and is illustrated in Figure 8G.

claim: ACSL4 may participate in the protein degradation system of LDs.
source: We propose that as an LDs enzyme, ACSL4 may participate in the protein degradation system of LDs. This is likely to be a novel function of ACSL4.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that ACSL4 regulates ZEB2 ubiquitination and is localized to LDs.

claim: LDs act as a platform for protein degradation.
source: Thus, it is likely that LDs act as a platform for protein degradation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ACSL4 regulates protein ubiquitination and is localized to LDs, and from the cited study showing LDs recruit proteins for degradation.

claim: ACSL4 may reduce the ubiquitin of ZEB2 via downregulating ubiquitin E3 ligase.
source: This result indicated that ACSL4 may reduce the ubiquitin of ZEB2 via downregulating ubiquitin E3 ligase.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-seq data showing that ubiquitin E3 ligases are reduced in ACSL4 knockdown cells.

claim: ACSL4 may regulate the ZEB2 mRNA level via lipid-epigenetic reprogramming mechanism.
source: We observed that ACSL4 can also promote FAO, which generates acetyl-CoA for the epigenetic regulation. It is likely that ACSL4 regulates the ZEB2 mRNA level via lipid-epigenetic reprogramming mechanism, which is worth studying in the future.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that ACSL4 promotes FAO and acetyl-CoA production, and on the cited study showing LDs-derived lipolysis provides acetyl-CoA for epigenetic regulation.

claim: ACSL4 located at the cytomembrane is likely responsible for dictating ferroptosis sensitivity by shaping the plasma membrane lipidome.
source: The cytomembrane ACSL4 is likely responsible for dictating ferroptosis sensitivity by shaping the plasma membrane lipidome, whereas ACSL4 localized to LDs has other functions.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that ACSL4 can be located at different cellular compartments and has different functions.

claim: ACSL4 localized to LDs is a pro-metastatic factor that promotes invasion and migration.
source: We provide evidence that ACSL4, which is located in LDs, is a pro-metastatic factor that promotes invasion and migration.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that ACSL4 co-localizes with LDs and promotes invasion and migration.

claim: ACSL4 and ZEB2 are preferentially expressed in BLBC cells and clinical samples that lacked ERα expression.
source: Furthermore, ACSL4 and ZEB2 were found to be preferentially expressed in BLBC cells and clinical samples that lacked ERα expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and immunohistochemistry data showing high ACSL4 and ZEB2 expression in ER-negative samples.

claim: Breast cancer patients with high expression of both ACSL4 and ZEB2 are associated with worse overall survival than those patients with low expression.
source: Survival analysis revealed that breast cancer patients with high expression of both ACSL4 and ZEB2 are associated with worse overall survival than those patients with low expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis data.

claim: ACSL4 and ZEB2 could specifically be used as prognostic markers for breast cancer.
source: Thus, ACSL4 and ZEB2 could specifically be used as prognostic markers for breast cancer, and this axes hold promise as a new metabolic therapeutic target for highly invasive breast cancer.
evidence: The claim is based on survival analysis data showing that high ACSL4 and ZEB2 expression is associated with worse prognosis.

claim: Breast cancer cells tend to store lipids in LDs for energy reserves.
source: Treatment with OA dramatically enhanced LDs abundance in the cells (Figure 4A), indicating that breast cancer cells tend to store lipids in LDs for energy reserves.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that exogenous OA treatment increases LDs accumulation.

claim: Lipids stored in LDs were utilized and degraded during cell migration and invasion.
source: In addition, we observed significantly reduced LDs in cells on the lower side of the transwell chamber, suggesting that lipids stored in LDs were utilized and degraded during cell migration and invasion (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that LDs decrease in cells after migration through a transwell chamber.

claim: ACSL4 upregulates CPT1A to stimulate FAO and ATP generation in BLBC cells.
source: All these results indicated that ACSL4 upregulates CPT1A to stimulate FAO and ATP generation in BLBC cells.
evidence: The claim is based on data showing that ACSL4 knockdown reduces CPT1A expression, FAO, and ATP production.

claim: Glucose metabolism is not involved in ACSL4- or ZEB2-mediated metabolic process.
source: To exclude OXPHOS derived from the aerobic glycolysis pathway, we measured lactate production and found no significant difference in lactate production between ACSL4 or ZEB2 knockdown and control cells, suggesting that glucose metabolism is not involved in ACSL4- or ZEB2-mediated metabolic process (Figure 5H, I).
evidence: The claim is based on lactate measurement data showing no difference between ACSL4/ZEB2 knockdown and control cells.

claim: The −287 E-box promoter region is essential for ZEB2-mediated ACSL4 promoter activation.
source: The luciferase reporter assay revealed that ACSL4 promoter activity was almost entirely abolished by the mutations (Figure 6H), suggesting that this promoter region is essential for ZEB2-mediated ACSL4 promoter activation.
evidence: The claim is based on luciferase reporter assay data showing that mutations in the −287 E-box abolish promoter activity.

claim: ACSL4 attenuated the ubiquitin proteolysis of ZEB2.
source: Conversely, we observed a increasing ubiquitination of ZEB2 in ACSL4 silencing cells (Figure 7D), suggesting that ACSL4 attenuated the ubiquitin proteolysis of ZEB2.
evidence: The claim is based on ubiquitination assay data showing increased ZEB2 ubiquitination in ACSL4 knockdown cells.

claim: ZEB2 and ACSL4 are present in a protein complex.
source: Notably, co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assays and GST pull down assays revealed a specific interaction between ACSL4 and ZEB2 proteins, supporting the notion that ZEB2 and ACSL4 are present in a protein complex (Figure 7E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on Co-IP and GST pull down assay data showing physical interaction between ACSL4 and ZEB2.

claim: ZEB2 mRNA levels were significantly reduced after ACSL4 knockdown.
source: This phenomenon could be explained by the fact that ZEB2 mRNA levels were significantly suppressed by the ACSL4 knockdown.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data showing reduced ZEB2 mRNA levels in ACSL4 knockdown cells.

claim: ACSL4 overexpressing cells show increased ZEB2 protein stability.
source: Conversely, ZEB2 protein maintained a relatively steady level at 6 hr in ACSL4 overexpressing cells compared with control cells that undergone obvious ZEB2 proteolysis at 4 hr after adding CHX, indicating an increased ZEB2 protein stability in ACSL4 overexpressing cells (Figure 7I, J).
evidence: The claim is based on cycloheximide chase assay data showing slower ZEB2 degradation in ACSL4 overexpressing cells.

claim: ACSL4 promotes breast cancer metastasis.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that ACSL4 promotes the lung metastasis of breast cancer cells in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo xenograft experiment data showing that ACSL4 knockdown reduces lung metastasis.
